title: Lesson 8: Champions and Power Users: Building an Internal Support Network
description: Champions and power users: why peer support outlives authority, how to select a support network by influence and representation rather than enthusiasm, and the three structures (regular gathering, defined support role, ongoing post-launch purpose) that let it run without the adoption owner.

questions.question: What distinguishes a champion from a power user?
options: A champion has the deeper technical command of the tool and all of its settings
A champion brings trust and influence, while a power user brings deep expertise
A champion writes policy, while a power user trains new staff
A champion is a manager, while a power user is an individual contributor
questions.explanation: A champion moves adoption through trust and example, while a power user moves it through practical command of a specific tool and workflow.

questions.question: A manager plans to appoint the three loudest volunteers as champions. What is the main problem?
options: Enthusiasm is not influence, and the network needs reach and available time
Three people is too many for a support network to coordinate well
Champions should always be chosen by seniority and tenure
Champions need a formal certification before they are allowed to help colleagues
questions.explanation: Selection works when it follows influence, representation across departments, and real bandwidth, not visible enthusiasm.

questions.question: Why should a support network keep operating after the implementation project closes?
options: To take over the vendor relationship and contract talks from the project team
To reduce the number of licenses the company needs to buy
Because value leaks after go-live, and peers tied to the work catch it
To train the next group of managers in how the tool is meant to be used
questions.explanation: A share of value is lost after implementation, so peers tied to the daily work, not the project, are what keep the new way alive.
